meta.name: Velo Ladder — fastball velocity benchmark snapshot
meta.source_of_truth: Notion: Second Brain / PPP / Velo Ladder (Sources + Velocity Ranges databases)
meta.access: COACH-ONLY. Do not expose to athletes, parents, or public routes.

row_type_values.anchor: Context only. Measured average, not a recruiting tier. Never classify against it.
row_type_values.secondary: Context only. Parallel tier taxonomy (spans multiple divisions). Never classify against it.

meta.null_band_meaning: No sourced data yet. Render as 'No data yet', never as 0 or blank.

sources.title: Next Commit — Pitcher Velocity Standards (Fastball MPH)
sources.author: Next Commit
sources.limitations_summary: Screenshot of an infographic with no methodology or sample size on the graphic. A later named-author NextCommit article says these are the same benchmarks as its standards page and cites Prep Baseball Report and Perfect Game showcase data as lineage (not linked, not independently verifiable). That later page merges NAIA and JUCO into one row, unlike this screenshot.

sources.title: TopVelocity — What Velocity to Get Recruited (College Standards)
sources.author: TopVelocity
sources.limitations_summary: Content marketing for a $99/mo training program. Says its table is synthesized from NCSA guidelines and unnamed analytics services, with no link or methodology. Incentive to make the velocity gap look large. Also cites Sakurai et al. 2024 (JSCR) on jump power vs velocity, which is not part of the ladder.

sources.title: WIN Reality — Pitching Velocity by Age: Average Fastball Benchmarks from Youth Baseball to MLB
sources.author: Andrew Don — WIN Reality
sources.limitations_summary: Commercial (VR hitting trainer). Named author and date, and it flags that showcase data skews high. Youth age bands are credited to TopVelocity, so they are not independent of that source. HS and college numbers are an unspecified blend. The MLB average trend (94.7 mph in 2026, 91.9 in 2008) is widely corroborated.

sources.title: Rapsodo — College Baseball Pitching Averages and How to Reach Them
sources.author: Rapsodo
sources.limitations_summary: Device-measured data, but pooled across JUCO to D1 rather than by division, no college-specific sample size, selection bias toward programs that own Rapsodo hardware, dated 2023. A measured average of pitchers, not a recruiting threshold. Also has spin and break data (out of scope). Mentions a gated guide covering ages 10 to pro.

sources.title: Go Big Recruiting — College Pitcher Tier Profiles
sources.author: Go Big Recruiting
sources.limitations_summary: No author, date, or methodology. Tiers span multiple NCAA divisions each, so they do not map onto the D1/D2/D3/NAIA/JUCO rows. Top tier states both an 84 floor and an 87 floor. Includes ERA, K/IP, BB/IP, and secondary-pitch benchmarks per tier (out of scope for the fastball-only ladder).

sources.title: NextCommit — Pitching Velocity by Age (12-18) + College Targets
sources.author: Adam Paganelli, Co-founder — NextCommit
sources.limitations_summary: Commercial lead-gen. Named author and dates, cites Prep Baseball Report and Perfect Game. College table is the same data as the NextCommit standards page (not independent). Merges NAIA and JUCO at 82-88. The age chart (12-18) gives Average vs Strong (~top quartile), which is closer to percentile-style data than most sources.

sources.title: Uncommitted U — Pitching Velocity Benchmarks by Level
sources.author: Wayne Keeton — Uncommitted U
sources.limitations_summary: Presented as a consensus of published charts. Discloses a small spot-check (37 showcase pitchers) and its limits, which is unusually transparent. Internally inconsistent on D1 (three different framings: qualitative band, roster average, recruiting threshold). Promotes its own tool.

sources.title: Joe Eisenmann — Chasing Velo: Benchmarks for 13-18 Year Old Competitive Pitchers
sources.author: Joe Eisenmann, PhD
sources.limitations_summary: Percentile methodology (25th/50th/75th/90th) and disclosed limitations. Peer-review status of the venue (Archives of IronMan Performance) is unverified. Data came from AI-assisted scraping of an unnamed showcase site, so it skews toward competitive athletes; cross-sectional design. The full percentile grid is a figure that was not extracted; only prose-stated numbers were used (13U: 60/65/70 at 25th/50th/75th; 50th-percentile pitcher reaches 87 at 18).

sources.title: Joe Eisenmann — Age- and Maturity-based Modeling of Fastball Velocity in 25 MLB Pitchers
sources.author: Joe Eisenmann, PhD
sources.limitations_summary: 154 observations across 25 MLB pitchers from Perfect Game, Baseball-Reference, and Baseball Savant. Same venue caveat as the other Eisenmann paper. This is an elite trajectory, not a typical range; the sample skews toward tall, early-maturing pitchers. Also finds velocity plateaus during the early-to-mid growth spurt (~85-91% adult height), then rises.

sources.title: Gene Coleman — How Hard Should You Throw?
sources.author: Gene Coleman, Ed.D., RSCC*E — Pro Baseball Strength & Conditioning Coaches Society
sources.limitations_summary: Credentialed author, but the age-band figures have no disclosed data source or methodology. Eisenmann's paper criticizes a Coleman article for unsourced averages, though the figures it quotes do not exactly match this piece. Gives college recruiting floors (D1 87+, D2 85+, D3/JUCO 82+; LHP 2-3 mph lower) consistent with the ladder.

sources.title: Premier Pitching — What Is the Average Baseball Pitch Speed?
sources.author: Premier Pitching Performance Team
sources.limitations_summary: No named author, date, or methodology; commercial remote-training site. Lumps D2/D3 at 85-90, which conflicts with the ladder's D3 range (78-86). Gives role splits (JV vs varsity, starter vs reliever, MLB starter 92-94 vs reliever 94-97) that the ladder does not model.

ranges.notes: Source gives a combined 9-10yo age band, mapped to 10U (WIN Reality, itself crediting TopVelocity's age chart). Premier Pitching gives a broader 10-12yo band (45-60, no single-age breakdown) — widened the ceiling to 60 to reflect it, though it's a less precise, wider bucket than the age-specific figure.
Source gives a combined 11-12yo age band (50-60, WIN Reality/TopVelocity). Premier Pitching gives a broader 10-12yo band (45-60, no single-age breakdown) — floor extended to 45 to reflect it.

WIN Reality gave a combined 11-12yo band (50-60). NextCommit's age-12 chart gives Average 50-58 / Strong 58-64. Coleman: early developers 57-61, late developers <55 — consistent, fits inside the existing range. Premier Pitching: 12yo specifically — "50-55 is right on track" — also consistent.

WIN Reality gave a combined 13-14yo band (60-75). NextCommit's age-13 chart gives Average 55-65 / Strong 65-70. Uncommitted U (age 13/8th grade): Average 55-65, Top 10% 70+. Eisenmann (PhD, percentile methodology): 25th pctile 60, 50th pctile 65, 75th pctile 70 — the strongest single data point in this row, lands cleanly inside the existing range. Eisenmann flags the 25th percentile as closer to a true population average than the 50th, since the underlying sample skews toward competitive/showcase athletes. Coleman: advanced 13yo 61-64, late developers <60 — also consistent.

WIN Reality gave a combined 13-14yo band (60-75). NextCommit's age-14 chart gives Average 60-70 / Strong 70-75. Uncommitted U (age 14/Freshman): Average 62-70, Top 10% 75+. Coleman: 14yo typically 65-69, trending into the 70s by year-end — consistent, fits inside the existing range.

Freshman (14-15yo) band per WIN Reality (65-75) and NextCommit age-15 (Average 65-74/Strong 74-80). Uncommitted U (age 15/Sophomore, note: their grade label runs a year ahead of this row's Freshman tag): Average 68-75, Top 10% 80+. Coleman: 15yo (freshman) 69-77, above-average size 80 — consistent, top end matches exactly.

Sophomore (15-16yo) band per WIN Reality (70-80) and NextCommit age-16 (Average 69-78/Strong 78-83). Uncommitted U (age 16/Junior): Average 73-80, Top 10% 85+ — extends the top end to 85. Also notes D1 interest generally begins around 85 mph with projection at this age. Coleman: 16yo average 73-78, 80+ starts drawing college scout attention — consistent.

Junior (16-17yo) band per WIN Reality (75-85) and NextCommit age-17 (Average 74-82/Strong 82-87). Uncommitted U (age 17): Average 76-83, Top 10% 87+ — lands inside existing range. Also gives the clearest single recruiting-threshold line seen yet at this age: "87+ D1, 82-87 D2/NAIA, 78-84 D3/JUCO, all with command" — consistent with the College rows already in this ladder. Coleman: 17yo average upper-70s/low-80s, larger/more mature 85-87 — top end matches exactly.

Senior (17-18yo) band per WIN Reality (80-90) and NextCommit age-18 (Average 78-85/Strong 85-92+). Uncommitted U (age 18): Average 78-85, Top 10% 90+. Eisenmann (PhD, percentile methodology): 50th percentile = 87 for a pitcher tracking that percentile from 13 to 18 — lands cleanly inside the existing range and is the strongest single data point here. Coleman: smaller/less-developed 18yo mid-to-upper 70s, larger 81-84, fully developed upper-80s/low-90s — floor extended to 75 to capture the smaller/less-developed sub-group Coleman describes.

Path to 4-year programs. Two sources roughly agree; range widened. Next Commit: RHP 82-88/LHP 80-86. TopVelocity: RHP 82-90/LHP 80-87. Cross-checked against a 3rd source (WIN Reality lumps NAIA/JUCO together: 82-88, combined/no hand split) — consistent, within this range. A newer Next Commit article also lumps NAIA/JUCO together at 82-88, matching this row's range.

Values pitching IQ and command. Two sources roughly agree; range widened. Next Commit: RHP 80-86/LHP 78-83. TopVelocity lumps D3/NAIA together: RHP 78-84/LHP 77-82. Cross-checked against a 3rd source (WIN Reality: 80-86, combined/no hand split) — consistent, within this range. A newer Next Commit article also lumps NAIA/JUCO together at 82-88, matching this row's range. CONFLICT FLAG: Premier Pitching lumps D2/D3 together at 85-90, notably higher than this row's 78-86 — kept the existing range since 4 sources converge on it and this is a single unnamed/uncited source, but worth knowing this disagreement exists if you ever see a D3 arm sitting 85+.

Competitive D2 programs. Two sources roughly agree; range widened. Next Commit: RHP 84-88/LHP 82-85. TopVelocity: RHP 84-90/LHP 82-87. Cross-checked against a 3rd source (WIN Reality: 84-88, combined/no hand split) — consistent, within this range.

Flexible scholarship options. Two sources roughly agree; range widened. Next Commit: RHP 80-86/LHP 78-84. TopVelocity lumps D3/NAIA together: RHP 78-84/LHP 77-82. Cross-checked against a 3rd source (WIN Reality lumps NAIA/JUCO together: 82-88, combined/no hand split) — consistent, within this range. Flag: a newer Next Commit article also lumps NAIA/JUCO together at 82-88, dropping the 80-86 floor this row (and the original Next Commit screenshot) uses for NAIA specifically — inconsistent with the publisher's own earlier page. Kept the lower floor here since it's more specific to NAIA alone.

Top 50 programs (SEC, Big Ten, Big 12, ACC). Two commercial sources roughly agree; range widened to cover both. Next Commit: RHP 92-97+/LHP 90-94. TopVelocity: RHP 90-95+/LHP 88-92+. Both top ends open-ended ("+"). Cross-checked against a 3rd source (WIN Reality), which cites a generic D1 range of 88-95+ without splitting by conference tier — consistent with this range.

Solid D1 programs. Two sources roughly agree; range widened. Next Commit: RHP 88-92/LHP 86-90. TopVelocity: RHP 88-91/LHP 85-89. Cross-checked against a 3rd source (WIN Reality), which cites a generic D1 range of 88-95+ without splitting by conference tier — consistent with this range.
Smaller D1 conferences. Only sourced from Next Commit — TopVelocity doesn't break out a Low-Major tier separately (it only splits D1 into Power Conf. and Mid-Major).

Average four-seam fastball, not a floor-to-ceiling range for any one pitcher. WIN Reality: 2026 league avg 94.7 mph, up from 94.5 the prior season and 91.9 mph in 2008 (first Statcast-era tracking season); 6th straight season of increases. Premier Pitching corroborates directionally (avg 93-94, "2-3 mph faster than 10-20 years ago") and adds a role split not previously captured: starters typically 92-94, relievers 94-97 — range widened to cover that full spread rather than just the blended average.

4-seam fastball average from actual Rapsodo device readings, pooled across JUCO through D1 (not split by tier). Single point average, not a range — same value in Low/High. This is a measured average of actual pitchers, not a recruiting-target threshold like the other College rows, so treat it as a sanity-check anchor rather than something to reconcile against those ranges directly: it sits below most of the division-tier ranges because it includes the full population using Rapsodo, not just recruitable arms.

ranges.level: College — Go Big Tier 1 (High D1 / Elite JUCO)
ranges.notes: No RHP/LHP split given. Bullet range 84-95+; source's own prose narrows this to "87 to 95 MPH on a consistent basis" for prototypical D1 recruits — both preserved here, treat 87 as the more realistic recurring floor. Non-velocity: 2 additional pitches thrown to spots consistently, ERA below 2.00, ≥1 K/IP, <0.5 BB/IP (walks less than 1 per 2 IP).

ranges.level: College — Go Big Tier 2 (Lower D1 / High D2 / NAIA / Lower JUCO)
ranges.notes: No RHP/LHP split given. Top end open-ended ("90+"). Spans four division labels in one bracket per the source — doesn't map 1:1 onto the D1/D2/NAIA/JUCO rows. Non-velocity: 1 additional pitch thrown to spots consistently, ERA below 3.00, ~1 K/IP, ~0.5 BB/IP (walks around 1 per 2 IP).

ranges.level: College — Go Big Tier 3 (Lower NAIA / D2)
ranges.notes: No RHP/LHP split given. Non-velocity: control of at least one off-speed pitch with a second in development, ERA 2.50-3.50, K:BB ratio of 1:1.
